title: The environment of relationships
header_line: My analysis of one book on habits. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: What does your circle say about the way you work with people?
A student defined codependence: you are both dependent on each other for something not authentic; you rely on a trigger and a response from the other, so you never build a deeper relationship.
Another said: good relationships improve you in an internal way; bad ones drag you back and do not let you try new things.
I said that when I go into someone's house I am observant: the objects, the books on the shelves, say who that person is.

I asked: when two people have good intentions to do business, where can intention go wrong? A student said: when you have the same end goal but the way to get there varies, which can lead to conflict.

I said: ask whether they have the resources and the perception to get there. How do they select people? Look at their track record: friends they keep in touch with, partnerships of ten or twenty years, against someone who is always blaming others.
A student said that a prejudiced person is someone who prejudges based on assumptions or things they have heard.

I said that we also make assumptions because we drag negative anchors and triggers. Suspend judgment, and still be careful: you could be intuitively right that someone is toxic for you. It is a thin line.
Whom do you avoid because of an assumption you have not tested?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write a relationship that improves you and why.
Write one that drags you back and how.
Write the track record you would check in a partner.
Write an assumption you have about someone.
Write how you could test it.

check.q: What did a student say about codependence?
choices: You rely on a trigger and response, not depth

check.q: What did I say objects in a house reveal?
What did a student say a prejudiced person does?

recap: Choose relationships that improve you. Check track records. Test your assumptions.
